.bashrc  /  PS1

Show the machine's IP address in your bash prompt

Four steps to replace the default user@host prompt with one that shows the box's actual IP address — useful when you're bouncing between VMs that all share the same hostname.

Shell: bash File: ~/.bashrc Editor: gedit
1

Open a terminal

Launch a terminal window. You'll land at your regular prompt, still showing the old host@(ip):~ $ format — that's what we're about to edit.

A fresh terminal window, sitting at the prompt.

2

Open .bashrc in gedit

Type the following and press Enter. This opens your personal bash config file in the graphical text editor.

gedit .bashrc

gedit .bashrc, typed at the prompt.

3

Find line 64 — the code that fetches the IP

Scroll (or use gedit's Go to Line) down to line 64. This is the block that actually computes the machine's IP address and builds it into the prompt:

IP=$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}') PS1="\h@($IP):\w \$"

Lines 64–71: the IP lookup, and the first PS1 override inside the else block.

Line 64 runs hostname -I (all IPs assigned to the host), pipes it through awk '{print $1}' to keep just the first one, and stores it in the variable $IP. Line 65 is already there by default and uses that variable to build the prompt — nothing to change here.

4

Comment out line 68 and add line 69

Line 68 is the distro's original, colorless PS1 definition (it starts with #PS1='[`date...). Put a # in front of it to comment it out, then add a new line 69 under it with the IP-aware prompt.

#PS1='[`date "+%D"`]${debian_chroot:+-($debian_chroot)}\u@\h:\w\$ ' PS1="\h@($IP):\w \$"

Line 68 commented out, line 69 added right beneath it.

Do the exact same thing further down for the xterm*|rxvt*) case: comment out line 76 (the original PS1="\[\e]0;... title-setting line) and add an identical line 77 underneath it.

#PS1="\[\e]0;${debian_chroot:+($debian_chroot)}\u@\h: \w\a\]$PS1" PS1="\h@($IP):\w \$"
Why both places? Line 65 fires for non‑interactive/dumb terminals, and the xterm/rxvt block (around line 74–78) fires specifically when $TERM matches xterm* or rxvt* — which covers most graphical terminal emulators. If you only patch one, the other terminal type falls back to the original user@host prompt.

What lines 69 and 77 actually do

Both lines are identical, which is exactly the point — the same prompt format is applied regardless of which branch of the if / case logic runs.

PS1="\h@($IP):\w \$"
  • \hHostname of the machine, up to the first dot — bash's built‑in escape for the host name.
  • @A literal "@" character, printed as-is.
  • ($IP)The shell variable set on line 64, wrapped in parentheses. Because the whole string is inside double quotes, $IP is expanded to the actual IP address at the moment .bashrc runs.
  • :\wA literal colon, followed by \w — bash's escape for the current working directory (shortened to ~ under your home folder).
  • \$Bash's "am I root?" escape: prints $ for a normal user, # for root.

So a session as user seeda on a box at 10.0.2.29, sitting in the home directory, renders as:

laxima@(10.0.2.29):~ $

Save the file (Ctrl+S) and either open a new terminal or run source ~/.bashrc in the current one to see the change take effect.
